title: How I built memory that forgets on purpose: 90 days to stale, 365 to gone, and a pin that never expires
summary:
How I built memory that forgets on purpose: 90 days to stale, 365 to gone, and a pin that never expires

Ankita AI is a desktop AI assistant by Krish Verma, and it remembers things about you — your preferences, your projects, the decisions you made last month. The problem with a companion that remembers everything is that it remembers everything forever. A fact you stated once, a year ago, in a context that no longer exists, still arrives in the model's context with the same authority as something you said yesterday. The assistant doesn't know it's stale. It just asserts it.

So I gave Ankita's memory an expiry date — two of them, actually — and a rule that nothing is ever deleted.

Two windows, not a delete button

The design lives in two config values in src/core/config.mjs:

memoryStaleDays: Math.min(3650, posInt(pick("MEMORY_STALE_DAYS"), 90)),
memoryForgetDays: Math.min(3650, posInt(pick("MEMORY_FORGET_DAYS"), 365)),

A fact untouched for 90 days is stale: it sinks to the bottom of recall results and is filtered out of default recall entirely. A fact untouched for 365 days is past the forget window: it drops out of normal results altogether. Both windows are configurable with env vars, both are capped at 3,650 days (ten years), and both can be turned off by setting them to 0.

The important part: neither window deletes anything. A stale fact is still on disk, still in the store, and one explicit flag — includeStale on the recall tool — brings it back. The comment above the filter says it plainly: "Old, rarely recalled facts sink but are never deleted; only an explicit ask returns them."

What counts as "touched"

Staleness is decided by isStale() in src/memory/memory-similarity.mjs:

export function isStale(fact, { staleDays, now = Date.now() } = {}) {
  if (!fact || fact.always === true) return false; // Pins are deliberate and permanent.
  const days = Number(staleDays);
  if (!Number.isFinite(days) || days <= 0) return false;
  const at = Date.parse(fact.lastRecalledAt || fact.updatedAt || fact.createdAt || '');
  if (!Number.isFinite(at)) return false;
  return now - at > days * 86400000;
}

Three decisions are doing the work here:

  1. Pins never go stale. A fact marked always is deliberate and permanent — the user chose to pin it, so silence doesn't erode it. Everything else ages.
  2. The clock is last recall, not last edit. The timestamp is lastRecalledAt, falling back to updatedAt, then createdAt. A fact you keep using stays fresh because you keep using it — recall is the ageing signal.
  3. The threshold is a hard line, not a decay. Past 90 days, the fact is stale. There is no "a bit stale" — the flag is binary, one comparison against days * 86400000.

Recall refreshes the clock — but only for what you actually saw

Every fact in the store carries lastRecalledAt and a recallCount, and recall updates both through touchRecalled() in src/memory/profile.mjs. Two details matter:

  • One batched write. A recall can touch many facts, but the store writes once, not once per fact. The ageing signal is bookkeeping; it shouldn't cost a write per row.
  • Only rows the caller actually received get touched. The model can't keep a fact alive by searching for something else. And if the calling context is read-only — a read-only subagent, for instance — the touch is skipped entirely. The comment in tools/personal/recall.mjs is explicit: "recall is advertised readOnly, and a read-only subagent must stay read-only: the ageing signal is bookkeeping, never worth violating that contract."

The ageing signal also surfaces to the model. Each recall row carries its confidence, its conflictsWith list, and its stale flag, and stale rows sort last in every ranking — semantic or lexical. The system prompt even counts them: the personal-memory block in src/core/agent.mjs reads "Personal memory store: N saved fact(s), M stale" so the model knows the store has entries it shouldn't trust blindly. And the automatic context builder, personalMemoryContext(), searches project notes and decisions too, not just personal facts, inside a 1,600-character budget — so a stale personal preference doesn't crowd out a fresh project decision.

Confidence doesn't age. That's the part I'm least sure about.

Every fact also carries a confidence from 0 to 1. The default is 1, with a comment that says why: "A direct user statement is treated as certain." Confidence is clamped on write, returned on every recall row, and otherwise left alone.

That means confidence never decays. A fact you stated once, confidently, a year ago keeps confidence 1 right up to the day it goes stale — and then the binary flag takes over. The number says "certain" while the flag says "don't use this." I chose the binary flag over a decay curve because a decaying number would silently downgrade the user's own words without telling them, and a number that drifts is harder to argue with than a flag you can see. But I'm not convinced the split is right: the confidence is the model's evidence about how sure the fact is, and age is evidence about whether it's still true. Right now the two never meet.

The honest limits

  • The two windows run on different clocks. Staleness keys on last recall (lastRecalledAt), but the 365-day forget window keys on last edit — withinForgetWindow() in recall.mjs compares row.at, which is updatedAt. A fact you recall every week but never edit still drops out of normal results a year after its last edit. That may be the right behaviour — a year without an edit is a year without the user reaffirming it — but the two windows disagreeing about what "touched" means is an inconsistency I haven't resolved, and I can see the argument that the forget window should use the same clock as the stale window.
  • Stale is binary. There is no gradient between fresh and stale, no "probably outdated" — a fact is either in play or it isn't. A gradient would be more honest about how memory actually fades, but it would also be a number the model could quietly round down.
  • Recall is the only thing that refreshes the clock. If the model never recalls a fact, it ages even if the user still holds it. The store can't know what the user still believes; it only knows what the assistant has surfaced.

Ankita is open source at https://github.com/akyourowngames/A.N.K.I.T.A, and the site is https://ankita-sable.vercel.app. The memory code is in src/memory/ and tools/personal/recall.mjs if you want to check the two windows against the code.

Tell me I'm wrong: is 90 days of silence the right line for "forgotten", or should a fact the user stated once — confidence 1, their own words — never go stale on its own? And should confidence decay with age, or is a binary flag the honest shape — a fact is either in play or it isn't?

— Krish Verma, creator of Ankita AI

title: I built a .env file my AI agent can use but never read
summary:
AI coding agents are great at calling APIs. To do that, they need API keys. And the easiest place to put a key is a .env file in the project, which the agent can read like any other file. From there the key ends up in the agent's context, in the chat history, in logs, and sometimes in code it writes.

I wanted my agent to use my secrets without ever seeing them. So I built facedown.

How it works

Secrets live in one file in your project, .env.facedown:

# @desc token for the GitHub API
# @allow api.github.com
GITHUB_TOKEN=enc:v2:8kZ0…
  • Names, notes and allowed sites are plain text. The agent reads them to know what exists.
  • Values are encrypted (AES-256-GCM). The key isn't in the project: it's in your home folder, locked to your Windows account with DPAPI.
  • There's no command that prints a value. A secret only ever goes to two places: the environment of a program you run, or an outgoing web request.

The agent gets MCP tools instead of the values:

  • run_with_secrets: runs a command with the keys it names as environment variables.
  • http_request: sends a request with {{GITHUB_TOKEN}} placeholders that facedown fills in.
  • add_key: opens a small window on your screen where you type the value.

Printing a secret is fine

Your code can log a secret while debugging. The output just shows which key it was:

[debug] using token ***GITHUB_TOKEN*** | as base64: ***GITHUB_TOKEN:base64***
facedown: note: hid the value of GITHUB_TOKEN (2x) in the output.

Base64, hex and every common URL encoding are caught. A random stress test throws thousands of secrets, encodings, split chunks and pauses at the cleaner on every commit. It already found one real leak (two overlapping secrets), which is fixed.

Each key has a list of sites

A key can only be sent to the hosts on its list. A new key has none. Adding a site opens a confirmation window that only a click on Allow approves; Enter means Cancel. And the list is part of the encryption: if something edits # @allow by hand, that key stops decrypting instead of being sent to the new site.

What it doesn't do

It's a seat belt, not a vault door. An agent with a full shell that is deliberately trying to steal a secret can get around it: it runs as you, so it could scramble the value before printing it, or unlock the key file the same way facedown does. The strongest setup is an agent with only the http_request tool and no shell. Then the allowed-sites list is a real wall.

Try to break it

I think the rest holds, so there's a challenge: a script puts a random flag into a demo vault (nobody ever sees it), and you try to get it out through normal use. Rules and setup: docs/CHALLENGE.md. Reports go through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting, and finders get credited.

Get it

  • Claude Code: /plugin install facedown --marketplace necromancer124/facedown
  • Anywhere else: npx facedown help, and facedown mcp for any MCP client. It's also in the official MCP Registry as io.github.necromancer124/facedown.
  • Windows for now; Linux and macOS are planned after 1.0. Node 20+, no dependencies, MIT.

Repo: https://github.com/necromancer124/facedown

Feedback welcome, especially "this broke" or "this was annoying" u know the good stuff.

title: Kagelin v1.52.0: Building Universal Migration & Zero-Knowledge Data Portability
summary:
Moving between productivity apps usually hurts. Proprietary formats, lost hierarchies, missing checklists, and vendor lock-in keep users tethered to legacy tools.
With Kagelin v1.52.0, our goal was simple: true data portability without compromising client-side privacy.
Here is an architectural walkthrough of how we built universal importers for Microsoft To Do, Google Tasks, and TickTick, introduced bitmask notification controls, and decoupled task schedules from deadlines.

1. Zero-Knowledge Client-Side Migration

Most migration workflows route your raw data or credentials through a backend parser. Because Kagelin operates under a local-first, privacy-first model, migrations run entirely in the browser.

External Backup → Client-side Sanitization → Data Normalization → Deduplication → Local Storage (IndexedDB + TanStack Query)

Supported Ingress Rails:

  • Microsoft To Do: Ingests lists, steps (subtasks), and completion states.
  • Google Tasks: Handles multi-level parent/child task hierarchies, note formatting, and completed timestamps.
  • TickTick: Ingests multi-column CSV exports, extracting checklist items and mapping them into native Kagelin steps.
  • Loop Habit Tracker: Promoted from beta to Stable, parsing raw SQLite .db archives via WebAssembly (sql.js) in-memory.

Before writing any records to storage, users get an interactive drill-down preview detailing total items, top-level tasks, step counts, detected projects, and duplicate warnings.

2. Granular Notification Days Using 7-Bit Masks

A common user request was the ability to silence task push alerts on specific days (e.g., mute work task notifications on weekends) without altering the task's schedule or due date. Instead of adding relational schedule tables, I implemented an efficient 7-bit day mask stored as an integer (0 to 127):

// Bit index corresponds to Date.getDay() (Sunday = 0, Saturday = 6)
export const REMINDER_ALL_DAYS = 127; // 0b1111111
export const REMINDER_WEEKDAYS = 62;  // 0b0111110 (Mon - Fri)
export const REMINDER_WEEKENDS = 65;  // 0b1000001 (Sun + Sat)
export const REMINDER_MUTED    = 0;   // 0b0000000

export function isReminderAllowed(reminderDays: number, date: Date): boolean {
const dayBit = 1 << date.getDay();
return (reminderDays & dayBit) !== 0;
}


This keeps the schema lightweight, queryable, and easily evaluated in our background service workers.

3. Standard RFC 5545 Calendar Export

Data portability is a two-way street. In v1.52.0, users can export their entire event timetable into standard .ics format.

The exporter serializes recurring rules, UTC timestamps, and event metadata directly into an RFC 5545 string without pulling in bulky external dependencies.

4. Disambiguating Lapsed Schedules from Overdue Deadlines

In earlier releases, an unfinished task scheduled for yesterday shared visual styling with a task whose hard deadline had passed.
In v1.52.0, we introduced orthogonal date classification:

  • Overdue Deadline (due_date < today): High urgency, rendered with alert/destructive badge styling.
  • Lapsed Schedule (do_date < today): Denotes a missed intended work session ("Needs rescheduling") rendered with a neutral dashed border chip.

Try Kagelin v1.52.0

Kagelin is open source and free to try in guest mode with zero sign-up required:

  • Web App: kagelin.app
  • GitHub: Achyuth072/kagelin
  • Full Changelog: v1.52.0 Release Notes

title: OpenStreamHub: Building a macOS App for Hardware That Only Speaks Windows
summary:
This autumn I ordered a Cooler Master MasterHUB when it was on sale. If you haven’t seen one: it’s a modular control deck - a base with modules plugged into it. Mine has a 15-key keypad with a little screen behind every key, a 3-knob module, a round dial with a display, five faders and a two-roller scroll module.

There was one catch, and I knew about it when ordering. I work mainly on a Mac, and the official software is Windows-only. Cooler Master's software page doesn't leave much room for interpretation: "Support for Windows 10 (64-bit) or later is required". A macOS version had been coming soon for a while, and then the device was marked as legacy. So much for that.

Without the software, the modules don't do much. They light up and play their built-in animations, but none of the keys does anything on your computer. Basically, a very nice-looking paperweight.

While the package was still on its way, I came across cooltek-sdk by projectzero7, a Rust SDK for these modules. How hard can it be to build an app on top of it?

Quite hard, as it turned out. But a bit over two weeks later, the first version of OpenStreamHub was out - an open-source SDK and macOS app for the MasterHUB, aiming for parity with the official Windows app, and then some. Five releases later, it has plugins, if / else keys, OBS controls, and a key that answers Claude Code's permission prompts (the app was built with Claude Code, so that one was kind of inevitable).

It's not affiliated with Cooler Master in any way.

Standing on Someone Else's SDK

projectzero7's SDK, together with its companion probe repository with notes on the knob module's feature reports and the keypad's output reports, was my starting point. My protocol docs still cite those notes in several places.

OpenStreamHub continues that repository instead of just depending on it. The original commits from July are still in the history, the Rust crates keep their cooltek-sdk names, and the MIT / Apache-2.0 license carries over.

Good question: why fork instead of sending pull requests upstream? The upstream repo hasn't moved since July, and what I was building wasn't really an SDK anymore. It was an SDK, plus a background service, a profile format and a desktop app on top. title: Building DeleteEXIF: Why Serverless Client-Side Metatada Stripping is the Future 🚀
summary:
As developers, we often build tools that solve problems, but occasionally, the standard solution introduces a new privacy flaw. Many existing EXIF & metadata removers require users to upload sensitive personal photographs to their servers just to parse and wipe the file properties. That completely defeats the purpose of privacy!

That’s why I built DeleteEXIF (https://deleteexif.com/), a lightweight, completely serverless metadata stripper that runs entirely on the client-side.

Using HTML5 APIs, JavaScript, and local canvas/exif parser libraries, the entire process takes place in the user’s browser. No data payload, zero server storage, and no backend vulnerability risk.

In this post, I discuss why processing image metadata client-side is crucial:

No database, no risk: Users are assured that their data isn't harvested or logged.

Resource Efficiency: Zero server processing costs. Browser-level computational power handle image loads instantly.

Modern Browser Capabilities: Working directly with binary file streams and recreating metadata-free buffers locally.

I'd love your feedback, code review, or suggestions for optimizing client-side performance even further!

title: Your collab messages sound like templates. Here's how to check
summary:
Most collaboration DMs fail for the same reason: they could have been sent to anyone. "Huge fan, love your content, let's collab?" tells the other person nothing about why you picked them, and nothing about what they would get.

I built a small Hermes skill, collab-outreach, to fix that. You give the agent your own notes on each creator: one specific piece of their work you really saw, why the audiences overlap, and what you offer. The agent drafts a short message from those facts only. It does not invent shared history or flatter on your behalf.

Then comes the part I find most useful: a tiny checker script that reads all your drafts in a CSV and flags the usual problems. Is the specific detail actually in the message? Is there an offer? One clear question? An easy way out? Does it lean on empty flattery or pressure phrases? And do two messages look suspiciously alike, which is the copy-paste smell recipients notice at once.

A quick example. A draft that says "Hi Bob, huge fan! Let's collaborate?" comes back flagged: no specific detail, generic flattery, no offer, no exit. A draft that names a video, says you can feature their recipe in your newsletter with a link back, asks one question and adds "no pressure if it's not a fit" passes.

It checks wording only, in English, and it never sends anything. You review and press send yourself. No API key, nothing to install beyond Python.

The skill is open source (MIT) in the hermes-skills library.

title: Why moving a Python diff parser to Rust made it 3.1x slower while one Git fix made it 4x faster
summary:
I have been building Athena, an offline Python tool that scans Git history to find broken callers across a codebase before you merge a pull request. On small repositories it felt instant. Once I pointed it at 1,000+ commits and thousands of files, a single cold scan took 30 to 45 seconds.

My first instinct was the usual one: rewrite the whole thing in Rust. After profiling the actual bottlenecks, I realized a full rewrite would throw away Python's rock-solid ast module and make contributing much harder. So I kept Python as the core and tried fixing only what the profiler flagged.

1. The biggest early win had nothing to do with Rust

Before writing any Rust code, I looked at where time was actually going. Our Git inspector was spawning a new git cat-file -s and git show subprocess for every changed file. Across hundreds of commits, OS process startup overhead dominated the whole runtime.

Switching to a single batched binary git cat-file --batch stream fixed it immediately:

Before: 1 subprocess per file (git show / cat-file -s) -> 12.74s
After:  1 batched git cat-file --batch stream          ->  3.17s (4.02x faster)

No language rewrite needed. Just fewer processes.

2. When porting Python to Rust actually makes it slower

Next, I ported our unified diff parser (parse_unified_diff_raw) to Rust via PyO3. Every test passed and all 229 recorded inputs matched Python identically. Then I ran the benchmark:

  • Pure Python: 1.6 ms
  • Rust (PyO3): 4.8 ms (3.1x slower)

Why did Rust lose? When Python calls a Rust function through PyO3, strings and lists have to cross the Foreign Function Interface (FFI) boundary. Parsing a unified diff is mostly lightweight string slicing, so converting and allocating those strings across Python and Rust cost more than the parsing work itself. I deleted that Rust port and kept diff parsing in Python.

3. Where Rust actually crushed Python

Rust paid off big on tight CPU loops where compute far outweighed FFI copying. Four hot kernels passed strict equivalence checks and stayed enabled (with FAST_ANYTHING_DISABLE=1 available anytime to toggle back to pure Python):

Kernel Speedup Parity Checks
redact_secrets 41x (237.3us -> 5.8us) 776/776 identical
score_graph_trigrams 8.8x (37.3ms -> 4.2ms) 330/330 identical
compute_community_assignments 3.5x (9.6ms -> 2.7ms) 206/206 identical
extract_structural_symbols_raw 1.9x (16.2us -> 8.6us) 800/800 identical

4. Verifying zero quality loss across 1,000+ commits

Speed means nothing if native ports silently change results, so I audited pure Python against the hybrid Rust build across three large public repositories over 1,000+ commits each:

Repository Commits Graph Build (Python -> Rust) Parity
google/flatbuffers 1,000 43.39s -> 1.62s (26.73x) 14/14 SHA-256 checks identical
NVIDIA/cuvs 1,472 29.89s -> 1.33s (22.48x) 14/14 SHA-256 checks identical
microsoft/playwright-python 1,000 45.78s -> 12.22s (3.75x) 14/14 SHA-256 checks identical

playwright-python saw a smaller jump because it is mostly Python files (where ast.parse stays in Python) and still iterates 100k+ edges in Python during queries.

Takeaway

If you have a slow Python CLI or developer tool, resist rewriting the whole codebase on day one. Batch your subprocess calls first, measure FFI copy costs carefully and only move the hot loops that actually benchmark faster.

All code, tests and benchmark scripts are open source under Apache-2.0 here: https://github.com/aaryanrwt/athena

My first instinct was the usual one: rewrite the whole thing in Rust. After profiling the actual bottlenecks, I realized a full rewrite would throw away Python's rock-solid ast module and make contributing much harder. So I kept Python as the core and tried fixing only what the profiler flagged.

1. The biggest early win had nothing to do with Rust

Before writing any Rust code, I looked at where time was actually going. Our Git inspector was spawning a new git cat-file -s and git show subprocess for every changed file. Across hundreds of commits, OS process startup overhead dominated the whole runtime.

Switching to a single batched binary git cat-file --batch stream fixed it immediately:

Before: 1 subprocess per file (git show / cat-file -s) -> 12.74s
After:  1 batched git cat-file --batch stream          ->  3.17s (4.02x faster)

No language rewrite needed. Just fewer processes.

2. When porting Python to Rust actually makes it slower

Next, I ported our unified diff parser (parse_unified_diff_raw) to Rust via PyO3. Every test passed and all 229 recorded inputs matched Python identically. Then I ran the benchmark:

  • Pure Python: 1.6 ms
  • Rust (PyO3): 4.8 ms (3.1x slower)

Why did Rust lose? When Python calls a Rust function through PyO3, strings and lists have to cross the Foreign Function Interface (FFI) boundary. Parsing a unified diff is mostly lightweight string slicing, so converting and allocating those strings across Python and Rust cost more than the parsing work itself. I deleted that Rust port and kept diff parsing in Python.

3. Where Rust actually crushed Python

Rust paid off big on tight CPU loops where compute far outweighed FFI copying. Four hot kernels passed strict equivalence checks and stayed enabled (with FAST_ANYTHING_DISABLE=1 available anytime to toggle back to pure Python):

Kernel Speedup Parity Checks
redact_secrets 41x (237.3us -> 5.8us) 776/776 identical
score_graph_trigrams 8.8x (37.3ms -> 4.2ms) 330/330 identical
compute_community_assignments 3.5x (9.6ms -> 2.7ms) 206/206 identical
extract_structural_symbols_raw 1.9x (16.2us -> 8.6us) 800/800 identical

4. Verifying zero quality loss across 1,000+ commits

Speed means nothing if native ports silently change results, so I audited pure Python against the hybrid Rust build across three large public repositories over 1,000+ commits each:

Repository Commits Graph Build (Python -> Rust) Parity
google/flatbuffers 1,000 43.39s -> 1.62s (26.73x) 14/14 SHA-256 checks identical
NVIDIA/cuvs 1,472 29.89s -> 1.33s (22.48x) 14/14 SHA-256 checks identical
microsoft/playwright-python 1,000 45.78s -> 12.22s (3.75x) 14/14 SHA-256 checks identical

playwright-python saw a smaller jump because it is mostly Python files (where ast.parse stays in Python) and still iterates 100k+ edges in Python during queries.

Takeaway

If you have a slow Python CLI or developer tool, resist rewriting the whole codebase on day one. Batch your subprocess calls first, measure FFI copy costs carefully and only move the hot loops that actually benchmark faster.

All code, tests and benchmark scripts are open source under Apache-2.0 here: https://github.com/aaryanrwt/athena

title: How Can You Evaluate the Buyer and Seller Workflows in a Fiverr Clone Demo?
summary:
Most founders judge marketplace software in about four minutes. They open the homepage, scroll the categories, see a few gig cards with prices and star ratings, and think, yes, this looks like Fiverr. Then they pay. The trouble shows up weeks later, when a real seller can't work out how to send a revised file, or the owner can't find where a disputed order is sitting.

A proper Fiverr clone demo can prevent that, but only if you use it like a buyer, a seller and an admin, not like a visitor. The market is worth the effort. Grand View Research puts freelance platforms at roughly USD 6.4 billion in 2025, heading toward USD 24 billion by 2033, while Mordor Intelligence estimates about USD 8.9 billion for 2026 alone. The numbers differ, as market numbers do. The direction doesn't. If you are still deciding whether to start, this guide to building a Fiverr-style marketplace covers the basics. What follows is about testing what you are about to buy.

Why Does a Fiverr Clone Demo Matter More Than a Feature List?

A feature list tells you what exists. It says nothing about how it behaves. "Order management" on a sales page can mean a full lifecycle with deadlines, deliveries and revisions, or it can mean a table of order numbers. You only find out by clicking through.

Gig marketplace software connects buyers who need a service with sellers who offer it, and it holds the money in between. That last part is where most of the risk sits.

Think of the demo as a rehearsal for your first 30 days live. Whatever feels clumsy now will feel worse when real users arrive. Upwork's Freelance Forward research reported that freelancers added USD 1.27 trillion to US earnings in 2023, so both sides of your marketplace already know what a polished experience feels like. Try to get three test logins: buyer, seller and admin. If the demo only gives you two, ask why.

How Do You Test the Buyer Journey in a Fiverr Clone Demo?

Pick a real task. Say you need a logo. Search for it, then filter by price and rating. Open a gig page and ask yourself one thing: can I tell what I get, how long it takes and what it costs in under a minute? Check the seller profile for reviews and portfolio samples. If packages exist, compare them side by side.

Then place an order. Stop at checkout and look at what the buyer sees before paying: the total, any service fee, and a line explaining how the money is held. After payment, check where the order appears, what status it shows and how the buyer sends requirements or files.

Watch for friction. A buyer who has to hunt for the message button will not hunt for long. Also test the custom route. Can a buyer post a request and receive offers from sellers? Sales pages often list this. Confirm it works instead of assuming.

Questions worth asking the provider: which of these steps work on mobile, can a buyer cancel, and what happens when a seller never responds?

How Do You Test the Seller Journey?

Switch to a seller account and create a gig from scratch. Time it. Write a title, choose a category, upload images, set three packages, add an extra and fix delivery times. Does each field explain itself? Does the gig go live at once or wait for admin approval, and can the owner switch that behaviour?

Then do the unglamorous parts. Edit a live gig. Pause it. Open an incoming order and read what the buyer asked for. Upload finished work. If the seller can't see the buyer's requirements clearly, deliveries go wrong and refunds follow. Finish on the earnings page: can the seller see pending money, available money and the commission taken?

Seller experience decides whether supply stays. You can buy traffic for buyers. You cannot easily win back good sellers who left because the dashboard fought them.

What Should You Check in Orders, Revisions and Messaging?

Run two orders. The first is the happy path: order, requirements, delivery, approval, review. The second is the bad one: late delivery, revision request, cancellation, dispute. Most founders skip the second, and the second is where a marketplace earns or loses trust.

Messaging matters more than it looks. Buyers ask questions before buying and renegotiate scope during the order. Check that chat handles files and images, that notifications actually arrive, and that the history stays attached to the order. When an admin settles a dispute, that conversation is the evidence.

Where the demo can't show something, treat it as a question. How many revisions does each package allow? Who sets deadline rules? What happens to the funds if a seller goes silent for a week? A vague reply is still a reply. Gaps here are common in budget scripts, and the trade-offs of cheap clone scripts are worth reading before you decide.

How Do Payments, Commission and Withdrawals Work?

Keep three numbers apart: what the buyer pays, what the platform keeps and what the seller earns. Place a test order for a round figure, say $100, and see whether every screen tells the same story. If the buyer, the seller and the admin each see a different total with no explanation, that is a support ticket waiting to happen.

Then check the settings. Can the owner set one commission for the whole marketplace, or different rates by category? How are withdrawals requested and approved? What does a refund do to the seller's earnings?

Be careful about who controls what. Gateway fees, payout timing and country coverage come from the payment provider. Commission rates are your own business decision. A demo shows the mechanism. It doesn't set your numbers, and anyone quoting a payout timeline from memory should be asked to show it in writing.

What Does the Admin Side Need on Day One?

Founders spend weeks on the buyer-facing site and ten minutes on the admin panel, which is where they will actually live. Many of the launch challenges in a new marketplace land on the admin's desk first.

On day one you need a short list: seller verification, gig approval, category management, visibility of orders and payments, commission controls and a way to resolve disputes. Revenue reports, featured listings and seller tiers matter too, but they become useful once traffic exists. Ask to watch an admin settle a disputed order from start to finish. A dashboard screenshot proves very little.

What Are the Other Options Besides a Ready-Made Script?

Best Freelancer Script is one example of the ready-made route. Its Fiverr clone package lists a web platform with buyer and seller dashboards, gig packages and extras, buyer requests, real-time chat, a dispute panel, commission settings by category, Android and iOS apps, source code ownership and a year of technical support, and it runs a public demo you can test against the steps above. Listed features still need confirming in the demo, like everything else.

Other routes exist. WordPress with a marketplace plugin stack is cheap to start and fine for a small pilot, but gig packages, held payments and disputes often depend on several plugins working together, and updates can break them. No-code builders launch fast without a developer, though monthly fees grow with usage and you rent the product instead of owning it. The SaaS versus self-hosted question is really about control and long-term cost. Custom development gives you full freedom, but it takes months and a serious budget before the first order is placed.

FAQs

What should I check before buying a Fiverr clone script?

Run a full order from search to review, then a failed order ending in a dispute. Check commission settings, the admin panel and what the licence says about source code.

How long should a demo test take?

A couple of hours is realistic if you complete the whole order lifecycle with buyer, seller and admin accounts. A ten-minute browse tells you almost nothing.

What should a seller dashboard include?

Gig creation with packages and extras, order tracking, delivery upload, messaging, and an earnings view showing pending funds, commission and withdrawals.

Can I customise the software for a niche?

Often yes, but ask who does the work, what it costs and whether the source code is yours to change. Niche categories and onboarding forms are the usual first edits.

Does a good demo mean the marketplace will succeed?

No. Software gives you the foundation. Success still depends on your niche, how you recruit sellers, how you find buyers and how well you handle support.

Software is the easy part to compare. A demo, used properly, shows you whether orders, money and disputes behave sensibly before real customers are involved. Test the bad path as hard as the good one, keep the three payment numbers apart and write down every question the demo couldn't answer.

Marketplaces tend to be won on operations, not on homepages. The founders who last usually spent their early weeks on seller quality and fast dispute handling, and they chose software that made those jobs lighter.

title: AsoBeast 2.0: redesigned open-source ASO tool with a keyword inspector
summary:
AsoBeast is an open source App Store Optimization (ASO) tool and keyword rank tracker for the Apple App Store and Google Play. It is built for indie developers, small studios and agencies, and you can self-host it with Docker or use the hosted version at asobeast.com. Version 2.0, released on November 24, 2026, is the biggest release so far: every screen is redesigned, a new keyword inspector looks up any keyword in any country without tracking it, and the audit tells you how ready your app is to be featured. Nothing breaks, so an upgrade from 1.x keeps your data, API scripts and MCP agents working.

Key takeaways

  • Every screen has a new look, and the daily pages open with what moved and what to do next.
  • The dashboard covers 7, 30 or 90 days and shows which app caused a dip.
  • Press any row on the keywords page to see its position, scores, history and the top 10 results in one sheet.
  • The Keyword inspector reads any keyword in any country straight from the store, without tracking it.
  • The audit adds a featuring readiness checklist for App Store apps.

A dashboard that starts with what moved

Pick the last 7, 30 or 90 days. One sentence at the top says which keywords climbed and fell, and four figures each draw their own chart when you select them. A By app list breaks the change down by app, so a dip in the chart comes with the name of the app behind it. Your keyword movers sit beside the actions to take next.

The app overview opens the same way, with visibility, share of voice, keywords in the top 10 and the store rating. Its chart marks the days your listing changed. Read the dashboard guide

A rebuilt keywords page

  • Press a keyword to open a sheet with its position, its scores and where they come from, its history next to your listing changes, the top 10 results and where the phrase sits in your listing. Arrows step to the next keyword.
  • The controls fit one row. A Change column, a 7 or 30 day trend line and the icons of the three top apps sit in a table that fits a small laptop.
  • The Discovered tab holds the discovered keywords, suggestions and keyword combinations, and you can track several suggestions at once.
  • On an App Store app, select keywords and choose Add to keyword field to send them to the iOS keyword field editor.

Read the keywords table guide

Keyword research without tracking: the keyword inspector

The Keyword inspector in the sidebar reads any keyword in any country straight from the store: the top 50 apps, the autocomplete, popularity, difficulty and opportunity, and how strong the top 10 are. Each inspection lands on a map next to the others, and inspecting the same keyword again shows what changed since last time. AI agents can run it too, through the inspect_keyword MCP tool. How the keyword inspector works

Check if your app is ready to be featured on the App Store

The audit now reads the public App Store page. It scores the preview video and adds a featuring readiness checklist next to the score: preview video, in-app events, ratings, updates, localizations and screenshots. With App Store Connect connected, it also checks your featuring nomination and promotional text. The changes feed records in-app events, featured stories and the Editors' Choice badge, for your apps and your competitors. Read about featuring readiness

How to try AsoBeast 2.0

Self-hosting takes three commands with the published Docker images:

curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AsoBeast/asobeast/v2.0.0/docker-compose.pull.yml
docker compose -f docker-compose.pull.yml pull
docker compose -f docker-compose.pull.yml up -d --wait

The quickstart takes you from there to your first imported app. Upgrading from 1.x runs six small database migrations on start, and Postgres now gets 512 MB, so plan for about 128 MB more RAM. Take a backup first. The release notes list every change.

To skip the server, start the hosted version. Its 7-day trial starts once you add a card, and nothing is charged if you cancel before day 7.

FAQ

Is AsoBeast 2.0 a breaking change?

No. The REST API, the shared types and the MCP tools only gain things, so scripts and agents built on 1.x keep working. The version is 2.0 because the whole interface changed.

Is AsoBeast free?

The open source edition is free to self-host under the AGPL-3.0 license. The hosted version at asobeast.com costs from $10 a month after a 7-day trial.

Is AsoBeast an alternative to AppTweak or AppFollow?

For keyword research and daily rank tracking, yes. AsoBeast tracks App Store and Google Play rankings per country, scores keywords with a published method and imports keyword lists exported from AppFollow, Astro and Sonar. It has no download or revenue estimates, and it checks the stores at a modest rate, so it suits a portfolio measured in apps rather than hundreds.

Does AsoBeast track Google Play as well as the App Store?

Yes. Rankings, the keyword inspector, competitors and alerts work for both stores, in every storefront you track. The featuring readiness check is for App Store apps.

Can I use AsoBeast from Claude, Cursor or another AI assistant?

Yes. AsoBeast ships an MCP server. Version 2.0 adds list_keyword_inspections and get_keyword_inspection for reading inspections, and inspect_keyword for agents allowed to make changes.

The code is on GitHub, the docs are at docs.asobeast.com, and questions and ideas are welcome in r/asobeast.

Self-hosting takes three commands with the published Docker images:

docker compose -f docker-compose.pull.yml pull
docker compose -f docker-compose.pull.yml up -d --wait

FAQ

Is AsoBeast 2.0 a breaking change?

No. The REST API, the shared types and the MCP tools only gain things, so scripts and agents built on 1.x keep working. The version is 2.0 because the whole interface changed.

Is AsoBeast free?

The open source edition is free to self-host under the AGPL-3.0 license. The hosted version at asobeast.com costs from $10 a month after a 7-day trial.

Is AsoBeast an alternative to AppTweak or AppFollow?

For keyword research and daily rank tracking, yes. AsoBeast tracks App Store and Google Play rankings per country, scores keywords with a published method and imports keyword lists exported from AppFollow, Astro and Sonar. It has no download or revenue estimates, and it checks the stores at a modest rate, so it suits a portfolio measured in apps rather than hundreds.

Does AsoBeast track Google Play as well as the App Store?

Yes. Rankings, the keyword inspector, competitors and alerts work for both stores, in every storefront you track. The featuring readiness check is for App Store apps.

Can I use AsoBeast from Claude, Cursor or another AI assistant?

Yes. AsoBeast ships an MCP server. Version 2.0 adds list_keyword_inspections and get_keyword_inspection for reading inspections, and inspect_keyword for agents allowed to make changes.

The code is on GitHub, the docs are at docs.asobeast.com, and questions and ideas are welcome in r/asobeast.
